en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section First Chapter
Is it the case that one abandons defilements bit by bit, piece by piece?
Yes, it is.
What does a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry abandon by the vision of suffering?

He abandons the view of a personal entity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), as well as the defilements associated with them, in part.
In one respect he is a stream-enterer, in one respect he is not a stream-enterer; in one respect he has attained and acquired the fruit of stream-entry.

He has attained it, realized it, entered upon it and dwells therein; he dwells having touched it with his body. He dwells having touched it with his body in one part, but not having touched it with his body in another part.
[There are those who are] "seven-times-at-most," "family-to-family," "one-seed," and those endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, in the Dhamma... [and so on].
[Is it the case that] one who is endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones within the Saṅgha... [is it the case that] he is not endowed with a portion of the virtues dear to the Noble Ones?
One should certainly not say so... [and so on].
What does one abandon by the vision of the origin?
One abandons the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt, and adherence to rules and observances, as well as the defilements associated with them, in part.
Thus, one is a stream-enterer in part, and not a stream-enterer in part... [and so on].
"One part is endowed with the virtues pleasing to the Noble Ones, while one part is not endowed with the virtues pleasing to the Noble Ones"?
One should certainly not say this...
[and so on] ...What does one abandon by the vision of cessation?
"One abandons doubt, adherence to rules and observances, and the defilements associated with them in one part [only].
Is it then the case that one is a stream-enterer in one part and not a stream-enterer in another part...
and so on... that one is endowed with the virtues pleasing to the Noble Ones in one part and not endowed with the virtues pleasing to the Noble Ones in another part?"
It should not be said thus...
[as before] ...What does one abandon through the vision of the Path?
One abandons adherence to rules and observances and the defilements associated therewith.
In one respect he is a stream-enterer, in another respect he is not a stream-enterer;

in one respect he has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon the fruit of stream-entry, dwelling having touched it with the body, while in another respect he does not dwell having touched it with the body;
in one respect he is "one who has seven births at most," "one who goes from family to family," or "one who has only one seed remaining"; [and he possesses] unwavering confidence in the Buddha.
Is one who is endowed with faith in the Dhamma … [and] in the Saṅgha … [and] endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones, not also endowed with a portion of those virtues dear to the noble ones?
It should not be stated thus... [etc.
...What does a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning abandon through the vision of suffering?
He abandons gross sensual lust, gross ill-will, and a portion of the defilements associated with them.
Is it the case that one part is a once-returner, one part is not a once-returner; and that one part has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon the fruit of once-returning,
dwelling having touched it with the body, while another part does not dwell having touched it with the body?
It should not be stated thus... [etc.
...What does one abandon through the vision of the origin?
One abandons gross sensual lust, gross ill will, and a portion of the defilements associated with them.
Is it the case that one part is a once-returner, one part is not a once-returner; and that one part has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon the fruit of once-returning,
dwelling having touched it with the body, while another part dwells without having touched it with the body?
It should not be stated thus... [as before] ...What does one abandon through the vision of cessation?
One abandons gross ill-will and abandons a portion of the defilements associated with it.
Is it the case that one part is a once-returner, one part is not a once-returner; and that one part has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon the fruit of once-returning,
dwelling having touched it with the body, while another part does not dwell having touched it with the body?
It should not be said so … [as before] … What does one abandon through the vision of the Path?
One abandons gross ill-will and the defilements associated with it.
Is it that one part is a once-returner, one part is not a once-returner, and one part has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon the fruit of once-returning,
dwelling having touched it with the body, while another part dwells without having touched it with the body?
It should not be said thus… [as before]… When a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) abandons what through the vision of suffering?
He abandons the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāga), the latent tendency of ill-will (byāpāda), and a portion of the defilements associated with them.
In one part he is a non-returner, in another part he is not a non-returner;

in one part he has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and dwells having entered upon the fruit of non-returning, dwelling having touched it with the body, while in another part he does not dwell having touched it with the body;
in one part he is one who attains nibbāna in the interval, one who attains nibbāna upon landing, or one who attains nibbāna without exertion.
"One who attains final nibbāna with exertion, one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm, and one who is not partially one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm"—
it should not be said thus...
[and so on] ...What does one abandon by the vision of the origin?
"He abandons desire for sensual pleasure that remains as a subtle residue; he abandons ill will that remains as a subtle residue, as well as a portion of the defilements associated with it.
Is it then the case that "one part is a non-returner, one part is not a non-returner...
[and so on] ... one part is one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm, one part is not one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm"?
It should not be stated thus... [etc.
...What does one abandon through the vision of cessation?
One abandons ill-will together with its subtle remnants, and one abandons a portion of the defilements associated with it.
“Is it the case that one part is a non-returner,
while another part is not a non-returner … [and so on] … that one part is one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm, while another part is not one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm?
“One should certainly not say so … [and so on].”
What does one abandon through the vision of the path?
One abandons the defilements associated with it.
In part he is a non-returner, in part he is not a non-returner; in part he has attained, acquired, and realized the fruit of non-returning.
Does one dwell having realized [the goal], having attained it, and dwelling having touched it with the body; or does one dwell having touched it with the body only in part?

Is there one who attains final nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyī*), one who attains final nibbāna upon arrival (*upahaccaparinibbāyī*), one who attains final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*), one who attains final nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*), one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (*uddhaṁsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī*), or one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm only in part?
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … When a person practicing for the realization of Arahatship abandons what through the vision of suffering?
He abandons attachment to the fine-material realm, attachment to the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, and a portion of the defilements associated with them.
In one respect he is an arahant; in one respect he is not an arahant. In one respect he has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon and dwells in arahantship;
he dwells having touched it with his body, while in one respect he does not dwell having touched it with his body.

In one respect he is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion; he has done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own goal, and completely exhausted the fetters of existence.
One who is liberated through right knowledge has lifted the crossbar, filled in the moat, pulled out the pillar, and is without a gate;
he is noble, with banner lowered, burden laid down, detached, a victor of well-won victory.

For him, suffering is fully understood, its origin abandoned, its cessation realized, and the path cultivated; that which is to be directly known has been directly known, and that which is to be fully understood has been fully understood.

"What is to be abandoned has been abandoned; what is to be developed has been developed; what is to be realized has been realized" (and "partially what is to be realized has been realized")—is it not the case that "partially what is to be realized has not been realized"?
One should certainly not say so... [etc.]
What does one abandon by the vision of the origin?
One abandons lust for the form realm and lust for the formless realm; one abandons pride, restlessness, ignorance, and the defilements associated with them, in part.
[In this regard] one is an Arahant in part, and not an Arahant in part... [etc.]
"One part of what is to be realized has been realized, while one part of what is to be realized has not been realized"?
One should certainly not say this...
[and so on] ...What does one abandon by the vision of cessation?
"He abandons conceit; he abandons restlessness, ignorance, and the defilements associated with them in part.
Is it the case that he is an Arahant in one respect and not an Arahant in another respect ... pe ...
that he has realized what is to be realized in one respect and has not realized what is to be realized in another respect?
It should not be said thus… [as before]… What does one abandon by the vision of the Path?
One abandons restlessness, ignorance, and the defilements associated with them.
In one respect he is an arahant; in one respect he is not an arahant. In one respect he has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon and dwells in the state of arahantship;
he dwells having touched it with his body, yet in one respect he does not dwell having touched it with his body.

In one respect he is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion; he has done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own goal, and utterly exhausted the fetters of existence.
One liberated through right knowledge has the crossbar lifted, the moat filled in, the pillar uprooted;
he is without a bolt, noble, with banner lowered, with burden laid down, detached, a victor in a well-fought victory.

For him, suffering is fully understood, its origin is abandoned, its cessation is realized, and the path is cultivated. What is to be directly known has been directly known; what is to be fully understood has been fully understood.
“Has that which is to be abandoned been abandoned? Has that which is to be developed been developed? Has that which is to be realized been realized?
Has one part of that which is to be realized been realized? Has one part of that which is to be realized not been realized?
One should not say so… [and so on].
Is it not to be said that "he abandons defilements bit by bit"?
Yes, it is.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“Gradually, little by little, moment by moment, the wise one, ... [should polish away his impurities] as a smith polishes silver.”?
"Just as a smith blows away the dross from silver,
so should one blow away one's own impurities.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes.
In that case, it should not be said:
“He abandons defilements bit by bit.”
"Does one abandon defilements bit by bit?
"Yes.
"Was it not said by the Blessed One:"
“For one who has attained the perfection of vision,
these three things are abandoned:
personality-belief, doubt, and— ”
Whatever rules and observances there may be,
he is liberated from the four states of misery and incapable of committing the six acts of immediate retribution.
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“He abandons defilements bit by bit.
Does he abandon defilements bit by bit? Yes.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, at whatever time the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arises in a noble disciple—
‘Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation’— with the arising of that vision, bhikkhus, three fetters are abandoned in the noble disciple:”
“Personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances”—
is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said that "one abandons defilements bit by bit.
The Discussion on Bit by Bit is finished.
